newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Yasin sees five pct GDP fall in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Yasin sees five pct GDP fall in 1996.

text.p: Russian gross domestic product is likely to fall five percent this year, but the overall economic situation now favours growth, Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said on Friday.

Industrial output in September was seven percent lower than a year earlier, after an eight percent fall in August, he told the State Duma lower house of parliament during a debate on the governemnt's austere 1997 budget draft.
But Yasin said inflation had fallen, the rouble had stabilised, foreign trade was in surplus and foreign exchange reserves stood at $14 billion.
"It's possible to say that we have a situation in the economy which is favourable for growth," he said. "On the other hand the country is living through an extremely acute crisis."
Yasin, highlighting inter-enterprise debt of 431.5 trillion roubles, said Russia was also crippled by a financial crisis.
The government was owed 90 trillion roubles in unpaid taxes, and off-budget funds, such as those for medical care and pensions funds were owed another 68 trillion.
Unpaid wages at the end of September totalled 40 trillion roubles, he said.
Yasin said interest rates could fall to 20-25 percent annual by the middle of next year, creating conditions to sort out the payments crisis.
At present enterprises must pay banks 80-100 percent annual for three-month rouble credits. Yields fell below 50 percent on the T-bill market this week for the first time since the market was set up.
Finance Minister Alexander Livshits told deputies that lower interest rates would not be enough to revive the economy.

"We will get out of the crisis when money which is available in the economy reaches producers. But even if the price of this money goes down to 20-25 percent a year doesn't mean that this money gets to the factories and everything revives," he said.
"For that measures of a non-economic nature are necessary so that banks want to direct their funds there, and enterprises can assimilate them."
Livshits said the government was planning to raise 41 trillion roubles next year under new tax legislation, some of which was rejected this week by deputies.
He said deputies would have to agree to other tax measures to replace this money, or cut spending.
The budget submitted to the Duma envisages spending of 524.34 trillion roubles, revenues of 433.64 trillion and a deficit of 90.70 trillion, or 3.3 percent of GDP.
But the Duma's influential budget committee has called for the budget to be rejected, and deputies are likely to return it to the government to be reworked.
